companyCaseStudy.title: How Zoom Scaled ~30x (10M → 300M daily participants) During the Pandemic — engineering tradeoffs, regional SFUs, and autoscaling the media plane
companyCaseStudy.summary: Zoom went from ~10M daily meeting participants to ~300M in a matter of weeks in early 2020. To avoid global outages they had to re-architecture the media plane, add regional relays, and massively expand autoscaling, delivering orders-of-magnitude more capacity while keeping join times and quality acceptable.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook
In early 2020 Zoom's usage exploded from ~10 million daily meeting participants to roughly 300 million daily participants (publicly reported). That is a ~30x jump in endpoints, meetings, NATs, audio/video sessions and real‑time signaling — overnight. The problem wasn't just more servers: it was more NATs, more small meetings, more concurrent peer connections, and an order‑of‑magnitude increase in global UDP traffic.

## Problem
- Scale: media (audio/video) is heavy and stateful. Media relays (SFUs/MCUs), NAT traversal, and bandwidth had to grow fast.
- Geography: meetings are global; long RTTs and cross‑continent media flows cause poor UX.
- Signaling load: signaling servers (join/leave/room metadata) and presence needed to handle millions of concurrent websockets and HTTP requests.
- Operational: capacity planning, autoscaling, and monitoring needed to go from tens to thousands of machines fast.

## Challenge
- Spiky, global traffic created hot spots — a single trending meeting could create concentrated load in one metro.
- Real‑time media requires low latency (UDP) and stable NAT traversal — TCP fallback harms UX.
- Rapid growth left little time for long, careful migrations; Zoom needed repeatable, automated ways to bring capacity online worldwide.

## Solution (what Zoom did, at a high level)
Zoom publicly described a multi‑pronged approach: expand media infrastructure (regional relays/SFUs), push signaling to cloud auto‑scale groups, optimize clients and server codecs, and improve observability and operational runbooks. The engineering pattern looked like this:

- Regional SFUs: move from centralized media relays to many regional SFU clusters to keep media local (reduce RTT and bandwidth through long transits).
- Autoscaling signaling: put signaling and meeting management behind autoscaling groups (cloud instances + containers) with aggressive scale‑up policies and pre‑warmed capacity.
- Traffic engineering & peering: increase cloud/backbone capacity via additional cloud regions and direct peering to major ISPs/CDNs.
- Client optimizations: reduce outbound bitrate defaults, adaptively lower video quality, and better CPU/codecs to reduce per‑call resource usage.
- Graceful features adjustments: temporarily disable or alter non‑critical features to reduce load (e.g., reduce default HD video, adjust background processing) until capacity could catch up.
- Observability & runbooks: expand telemetry, dashboards and SLOs to detect hotspots quickly and route realtime ops to engineers with playbooks for rapid mitigation.

### Architectural decisions (visual)

```mermaid
graph LR
  ClientA[Client (Web/Mobile/SDK)] -->|WebSocket/HTTPS| EdgeSIGN[Edge Signaling Cluster]
  ClientB --> EdgeSIGN
  EdgeSIGN --> LB[Global LB / Edge Router]
  LB --> SIG1[Signaling Autoscale Group - Region A]
  LB --> SIG2[Signaling Autoscale Group - Region B]
  ClientA -->|UDP (SRTP)| SFU_EDGE_A[Regional SFU Cluster A]
  ClientB -->|UDP (SRTP)| SFU_EDGE_B[Regional SFU Cluster B]
  SFU_EDGE_A --> CentralSvc[Meeting Index / Metadata DB]
  SFU_EDGE_B --> CentralSvc
  CentralSvc --> MetricsDB[Timeseries / Telemetry (Prometheus/TSDB)]
  CentralSvc --> Logging[Elastic / Kafka]
```

- Signaling is horizontally autoscaled and stateless where possible; state is stored in central metadata services and fast caches.
- Media handled by many regional SFU clusters to keep RTP flows local to participants and reduce transcontinental hops.

### Concrete technical moves
- Pre‑warmed capacity: Zoom pre‑allocated additional VM instances and containers in priority cloud regions (and executed bulk instance launches with infra as code) so scale‑up was fast and predictable.
- Aggressive autoscaling policies: short evaluation windows and larger step‑up sizes for scale‑up; conservative scale‑down to avoid oscillation.
- Codec and bitrate defaults: defaulted to lower resolutions and introduced more aggressive adaptive bitrate rules to drop to audio‑only on constrained paths.
- UDP-first and optimized TURN capacities: increased regional TURN/SRTP relays to avoid TCP fallback and tuned keepalives/ICE timeouts to reduce churn from NATs.
- Better per‑call resource accounting: tracked CPU/memory per conference on SFUs to make bin‑packing more efficient — more meetings per instance.

### Before / After (high level comparison)

| Metric | Before (pre-surge) | After (during/after changes) |
|--------|--------------------:|-----------------------------:|
| Daily participants (public) | ~10M | ~300M |
| Global SFU count (approx) | Hundreds (regional) | Thousands (more regional clusters) |
| Median join time (typical) | Higher, with regional variance | Reduced for local meetings (fewer cross‑continent hops) |
| Default video bitrate per call | Higher (more HD) | Lower (adaptive defaults to favor connection success) |
| Incidents due to capacity shortage | Occasional | Rapid scaling & fewer site‑wide outages after measures |

> Note: daily participant numbers are those publicly reported by Zoom during their early‑2020 growth; exact internal SFU counts and join time numbers are operational details Zoom adjusted continuously.

## Results
- Zoom handled a sustained, multi‑week surge and supported hundreds of millions of daily participants without a total service collapse.
- User experience improved where regional SFUs were available (less jitter, fewer disconnects) — a clear win from moving media closer to users.
- Operational posture moved from capex‑style planning to rapid elastic cloud expansion and playbook driven incident response.

## Lessons & Tradeoffs
- Locality > Centralization: for real‑time media, move media processing closer to participants to cut RTT and reduce backbone egress.
- Autoscale is necessary but pre‑warming matters: aggressive autoscaling must be paired with pre‑allocated capacity for rapid, global surges.
- UX vs Quality defaults: temporarily lowering default bitrates/resolution preserves connectivity during spikes and is a better UX tradeoff than many disconnects.
- Observability is critical: telemetry and SLOs at all layers (signaling, SFU, TURN, client) enable fast diagnosis and targeted capacity increases.

## Practical checklist (if you face a similar 10–30x surge)
1. Identify the media path (who relays media?). Add regional relays to keep traffic local.  
2. Autoscale signaling with pre‑warmed instances and short scale‑up windows.  
3. Add peering/edge capacity and increase TURN server pool (UDP only where possible).  
4. Reduce default bitrates and enable aggressive ABR on clients.  
5. Expand telemetry and prepare on‑call runbooks for targeted mitigations.

## Epilogue
Zoom’s rapid growth was both an infrastructure and human challenge. The engineering response — regionalize the media plane, automate scale, and trade some video quality for connection reliability — is a useful pattern for any realtime system that needs to survive sudden, global adoption.
keyTakeaways: For real‑time media, locality matters: regional SFUs/TURN reduce latency and bandwidth costs compared to centralized relays.
Autoscaling must be complemented by pre‑warming and short scale‑up policies for rapid global surges; conservative scale‑down prevents oscillation.
When capacity is constrained, dropping quality defaults (bitrate/resolution) preserves connectivity — better UX than frequent disconnects.

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: signaling-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: signaling-deployment
  minReplicas: 10
  maxReplicas: 500
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 60

concept.title: How Raft Keeps Distributed Systems in Agreement — a Practical Guide to Consensus
concept.summary: When multiple machines must agree on a sequence of operations (logs, config changes, leader selection), things get messy fast. Raft is a pragmatic consensus algorithm that makes distributed agreement understandable, implementable, and robust for real systems.
concept.explanation:
## Why it matters

Distributed systems need a single source of truth. Without consensus you get split-brain, lost updates, and systems that behave differently depending on which node you hit. Raft gives you a concrete recipe so a cluster of machines can elect a leader, agree on a replicated log, and make sure every committed entry is applied in the same order.

**Analogy: An orchestra with a conductor**

- Imagine an orchestra with no conductor. Everyone tries to lead and the music falls apart. Raft chooses a conductor (leader) who decides what notes (log entries) to play. The other musicians (followers) copy the conductor and acknowledge. If the conductor disappears, the orchestra elects a new one.

---

## High-level overview

- **Leader election:** Nodes elect one leader. The leader handles client requests.
- **Log replication:** The leader appends client commands to its log and replicates them to followers.
- **Safety / Commitment:** An entry is considered committed when a majority has replicated it; only committed entries are applied to the state machine.
- **Fault tolerance:** As long as a majority of nodes are available, Raft makes progress.

### Sequence: client write through leader

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Leader: PUT /order {id:42}
  Leader->>Followers: AppendEntries(term, prevIndex, [entry])
  Followers-->>Leader: Ack
  Leader-->>Client: 200 OK (committed)
```

### Flow: leader election (simplified)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Timeout] --> B{No heartbeats}
  B -->|true| C[Candidacy: increment term, vote for self]
  C --> D[Send RequestVote to peers]
  D --> E{Majority votes?}
  E -->|Yes| F[Become leader: send heartbeats]
  E -->|No| G[Retry after randomized timeout]
```

---

## Before / After: what Raft fixes

| Problem | Without consensus | With Raft (leader + majority commit) |
|---------|-------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Conflicting updates | Race conditions, last-writer wins or random | Single leader serializes updates, deterministic order |
| Split-brain | Multiple nodes think they are primary | Only one leader per term; majority prevents split-brain |
| Durability | Lost writes if leader dies before replication | Writes replicated to majority before commit |
| Recovery | Hard to reconcile divergent states | Log-based recovery and snapshotting restore state reliably |

---

## Practical example: a tiny Raft-like loop (Python pseudocode)

```python
# Very small, not production-ready pseudocode showing heartbeats and append
class Node:
    def __init__(self, id):
        self.id = id
        self.current_term = 0
        self.voted_for = None
        self.log = []
        self.leader = None

    def on_timeout(self):
        # start election
        self.current_term += 1
        self.voted_for = self.id
        votes = 1
        for peer in peers:
            if peer.request_vote(self.current_term, self.id):
                votes += 1
        if votes > len(peers) // 2:
            self.become_leader()

    def become_leader(self):
        self.leader = self.id
        # send initial empty AppendEntries as heartbeat
        for peer in peers:
            peer.append_entries(self.current_term, [])

    def append_entries(self, term, entries):
        if term >= self.current_term:
            self.current_term = term
            # append entries to log (simplified)
            self.log.extend(entries)
            return True
        return False
```

*This snippet demonstrates the control flow — real Raft includes many more details: prevLog index/term checks, commit index advancement, RPC timeouts, persistent storage, and log compaction.*

---

## When to use Raft

- You need a strongly consistent replicated state machine (e.g., leader election, metadata store, coordination service).
- You can accept availability tradeoffs: if a majority is down, the cluster becomes read-only/unavailable for writes.
- You prefer understandable correctness over raw performance hacks.

Use alternatives (or eventual consistency) when low-latency writes on partitioned networks or multi-master without coordination are required.

---

## Common pitfalls and how to avoid them

- **Assuming fast elections without tuning timeouts.** Use randomized election timeouts to reduce split votes; tune according to network latency.
- **Forgetting persistence.** Term and log entries must be persisted to survive crashes; otherwise safety is broken.
- **Neglecting log compaction.** Logs grow forever — implement snapshotting to trim logs and speed recovery.
- **Not handling membership changes safely.** Use joint consensus (two-phase configuration change) instead of naive add/remove.
- **Expecting linear scale.** Raft is for coordination and metadata; replicating large payloads to many nodes hurts performance. Keep logs small or store payloads elsewhere with references.

---

## Operational tips

- Run an odd number of nodes (3 or 5) to maximize availability per node cost.
- Monitor leader latency, election frequency, commit index lag, and RPC timeouts.
- Test partitions and leader crashes in chaos-style drills.
- Consider libs: etcd/raft, HashiCorp Raft (go-raft), or use mature systems (etcd, Consul) unless you need a custom implementation.

---

## Final thoughts

Raft turns a hairy theoretical problem into an engineer-friendly recipe: elect a leader, replicate a log, and commit with a majority. The devil is in the implementation details (persistence, snapshots, membership changes), but once those are addressed, you get a simple mental model and a very practical consensus system.
keyTakeaways: Raft provides a clear, implementable recipe for leader election and replicated logs so a cluster can agree on state.
Safety depends on majority replication and durable storage; availability depends on cluster size and network health.
Watch the operational details: timeouts, persistence, log compaction, and safe membership changes are easy to get wrong.
